title: Extensive & Autonomous Listening

pts: Learners can control reading pace by rereading; spoken input passes at a fixed pace they can't control without technology.
Extensive listening programmes only became broadly practical with the spread of accessible audio technology.
This makes deliberate programme design, not just 'more listening,' the key lever now available.

v: A short audio clip at natural speed and its transcript

items: Listen once to a 60-second clip without the transcript and note what you understood.
Read the transcript at your own pace and note what you understood.
Compare: where did listening break down? Speed, unknown words, accent, words running together?
Discuss what this means for learners at lower levels.
Agree one change to how listening is set as homework.
Repeat with a clip in a language you know less well, to feel the learner’s experience.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: In reading I could go back; in listening, one missed word made me lose the next sentence.
I knew all the words in the transcript but didn’t recognize some of them in speech.

blocks.x: The second note matters. Recognizing a known word in fast speech is a separate skill from knowing it in print (Field 2008). Only listening builds it.

Purpose: to contrast reading and listening. Content: on the left, a learner turning back the pages of a book at leisure; on the right, a learner on a riverbank as words float past quickly on the water. Style: clean, gentle. Board version: an open book beside wavy lines with words on them.

items: VLC media player (free) to play clips and view transcripts together.

blocks.x: The teacher reads a passage aloud once at natural speed, then shows the text.

pts: Easy, self-selected audio at a comfortable level, for general understanding, without a follow-up test — the same core principles as extensive reading.
'Easy' for listening means both linguistic level and audio clarity — accent, background noise, and speed all matter.
As with reading, deviating toward intensive-listening habits (constant pausing, transcribing) loses the extensive method's distinct benefit.

v: Three short audio clips at different levels

items: Play 30 seconds of three clips.
After each, learners rate it: easy and clear, OK with effort, too hard.
Discuss what made each easy or hard: speed, vocabulary, accent, background noise, number of speakers.
Learners write their own rule: ‘A good extensive listening text for me is…’
Use these ratings to guide individual choices.
Learners rate clips they find themselves and share the best ‘easy’ ones.
Support: clips with pictures or video to support meaning.
Challenge: learners explain their ratings using terms from this unit (speed, clarity, accent).

blocks.x: A learner rule (written for this book):

lines: I can understand almost everything, I don’t need to stop it often, and I want to keep listening.

blocks.x: The principles are those of extensive reading (Unit 31): easy, self-selected, for general understanding and without a test. ‘Easy’ for listening includes audio quality. A clearly recorded story with one speaker can be easier than a simpler conversation recorded in a noisy canteen.

body: Purpose: to show the factors affecting listening difficulty. Content: a sound-mixer desk with five sliders labelled speed, vocabulary, accent familiarity, background noise and number of speakers, each moveable between ‘easy’ and ‘hard’. Style: clean, technical but friendly. Board version: five lines with sliders.

pts: Graded readers with accompanying audio give a reliable, level-matched starting point for extensive listening.
Podcasts and videos designed for language learners offer a wider, more current range once learners are ready for it.
Authentic native-speed media becomes appropriate progressively, not as the default starting point.

items: Share a three-rung list of sources with learners (see model language).
Learners start on the rung that matches their level.
They move up when material on their rung feels consistently easy.
Review the ladder each term and add sources learners recommend.
Divide sources by interest (sport, science, stories, music) as well as by level.
Support: learners at A1 begin with read-along audio and picture books.
Challenge: B2 learners add one authentic source at natural speed each week.

lines: Rung 1: graded readers with audio; read-along stories.
Rung 2: podcasts and videos made for learners (for example, BBC Learning English or VOA Learning English).
Rung 3: authentic media: news, interviews, podcasts for general audiences.

blocks.x: Authentic, native-speed media is a destination, not a starting point. Indian English sources such as radio news and interviews with public figures are valuable here, since learners will hear Indian English far more than any other variety.

body: Purpose: to show progression from graded to authentic input. Content: a three-rung ladder: the lowest rung shows a book with headphones, the middle a microphone labelled ‘for learners’, the top a radio and a phone showing a podcast. A learner climbs. Style: bright, encouraging. Board version: three horizontal lines with labels.

items: BBC Learning English (free); VOA Learning English (free).
News on AIR app (free) for Indian radio news. [VERIFY current availability of English bulletins]

blocks.x: Audio files copied to a shared school device or played through a speaker in class.

pts: Teach learners to use playback controls — replaying, slowing slightly — as a legitimate strategy, not a sign of failure.
Over-reliance on subtitles can substitute reading for listening; use them deliberately, not as a permanent crutch.
This connects to Unit 19's self-study strategy training, applied specifically to listening.

v: One device with a projector or speaker; a short video with subtitles

items: Play a short clip once without stopping.
Show how to replay a difficult 10 seconds, and how to slow playback slightly.
Demonstrate the ‘subtitle sandwich’: listen without subtitles, then with English subtitles, then without again.
Learners practise in pairs on a shared device or with the teacher controlling playback.
Discuss: when does using subtitles help, and when does it become reading instead of listening?
Learners set a personal rule: ‘No more than two replays per minute of audio.’
Support: allow home-language subtitles for the first viewing of harder content.
Challenge: no subtitles; one replay only.

lines: T: Where did you get lost?
S1: After ‘on the other hand’. Too fast.
T: Replay from there, at 0.9 speed. Better?
S1: Yes. ‘On the other hand, the rain helped the farmers.’

blocks.x: Replaying is a strategy, not a failure. Self-study strategies from Unit 19 apply here. Slowing speech a little can help, but very slow playback distorts it; keep speed changes small. Subtitles support learning, but a learner who always reads them is practising reading.

body: Purpose: to show strategic subtitle use. Content: a three-layer sandwich: bottom slice ‘Listen: no subtitles’, filling ‘Listen with English subtitles’, top slice ‘Listen again: no subtitles’. Style: playful. Board version: three stacked rectangles.

items: YouTube (free) for playback speed and captions.
VLC media player (free) for speed control on downloaded files.

blocks.x: The teacher rereads a sentence aloud on request, more slowly.

body: Show learners the playback controls on the devices they actually have at home. Many learners do not know that the speed can be changed or that a clip can be skipped back ten seconds.

pts: Short, frequent listening sessions build the habit more reliably than occasional long ones.
A simple log — source, duration, general topic — tracks engagement without testing comprehension in detail.
This mirrors Unit 31's tracking approach, adapted for audio.

items: Learners commit to about ten minutes of listening a day, five days a week.
They record source, minutes and topic in a simple log.
Once a week, in pairs, they tell a partner about one thing they heard.
The teacher checks logs occasionally for regularity, not accuracy.
After four weeks, learners review their totals and set a new target.
A class ‘listening minutes’ chart, with no individual rankings.
Support: shorter sessions (five minutes); the same story heard several times.
Challenge: longer sessions; learners add a one-line summary.

lines: Mon | BBC Learning English | 10 min | why we yawn
Tue | graded reader audio | 12 min | chapter 3, the storm

blocks.x: Short, frequent sessions build the habit more reliably than a single long session at the weekend. The log mirrors the reading log in Unit 31.

body: Purpose: to show frequency over intensity. Content: two calendars. One has a large block on Sunday only; the other has a small headphone icon on every weekday. A growing plant sits beside the second calendar. Style: clean. Board version: two weekly grids.

items: Google Forms (free) for a digital listening log.

blocks.x: A paper log page in the English notebook.

points.h: Listening for Pleasure vs. for Study
pts: Extensive listening for pleasure — music, podcasts on personal interests — builds volume and motivation simultaneously.
This complements, rather than replaces, the more structured listening work from Unit 3's staged listening lessons.
Motivation (Unit 22) is often easier to sustain here than with assigned intensive listening tasks.

items: Learners list what they already enjoy listening to, in any language.
They find one English source on a similar topic (cricket commentary, songs, science, stories).
In groups, they share and explain their choice.
The class builds a shared list of ‘listening for pleasure’ sources.
Staged listening lessons (Unit 3) continue in class; pleasure listening runs alongside them.
A song of the week, chosen by a different learner each week.
Support: suggest three starter sources for each interest.
Challenge: learners review a podcast episode for the class.

lines: A: I like cricket commentary in Kannada.
B: Try English commentary on the radio. You already know what’s happening, so it’s easier.

blocks.x: Choosing material that matches existing interests lowers effort and raises motivation (Unit 22). Background knowledge from home-language listening makes English input more comprehensible.

body: Purpose: to show pleasure and study listening side by side. Content: a split scene: on the left, a learner relaxing with headphones under a tree; on the right, a class completing a staged listening task with a worksheet. A bridge joins them. Style: warm. Board version: two boxes joined by an arrow.

items: Spotify (free with advertisements) for podcasts and songs.

blocks.x: Radio at home; songs sung in class.

pts: High-volume listening reinforces recognition of the connected-speech features taught explicitly in Unit 4.
Repeated natural exposure builds the automatic recognition that explicit teaching alone struggles to fully achieve.
This makes extensive listening a natural complement to, not a substitute for, focused pronunciation work.

v: A short clip learners have already heard extensively

items: Remind learners of one connected-speech feature from Unit 4 (for example, linking consonant to vowel).
Play a familiar clip; learners raise a hand when they hear an example.
Write examples on the board and practise saying them.
Learners listen for the feature during their extensive listening that week.
Focus on a different feature each week: weak forms, elision, contractions.
Support: provide a gapped transcript with the phrases to find.
Challenge: learners collect examples from their own listening.

blocks.x: Explicit teaching helps learners notice these features; high-volume listening builds the automatic recognition that one lesson cannot. The two work together.

body: Purpose: to show linking in connected speech. Content: three words (turn it off) drawn as characters holding hands, with a curved linking line beneath and the phonemic transcription above. Style: playful. Board version: the phrase with linking arcs.

items: YouGlish (free) for hearing a phrase in many real recordings.

blocks.x: The teacher models careful and connected versions aloud.

body: Learners often know a word perfectly on paper but fail to recognize it in speech because its spoken form changes in context. Field (2008) treats this recognition of words in connected speech as a key listening skill to train, not just a vocabulary problem.

pts: Share personal listening recommendations regularly, the audio equivalent of Unit 31's book talks.
Model the habit yourself — a teacher who visibly listens extensively signals its value more than any instruction alone.
Treat extensive listening as core curriculum time, not an optional extra squeezed in if time allows.

items: Choose one English source you enjoy and listen to it regularly.
Once a week, tell the class about something you heard, in two minutes.
Invite learners to share their own recommendations.
Display a ‘class playlist’ of recommended sources.
Review the playlist each term; drop sources nobody uses.
A monthly ‘listening café’ lesson where learners share clips in small groups.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: This week I listened to a podcast about monsoon forecasting. I didn’t know that… Has anyone heard something interesting?

blocks.x: A teacher who listens and talks about it shows that listening is part of life, not only an exam section. Treat listening time as curriculum time, as Unit 31 does for reading.

body: Purpose: to show a shared listening culture. Content: a large wall chart shaped like a music player screen, listing podcast and audiobook titles with small learner names beside each recommendation. Style: modern, bright. Board version: a list with speaker icons.

items: Padlet (free plan) for a shared playlist.

blocks.x: A chart-paper playlist on the classroom wall.

body: For two weeks, spend two minutes each Monday telling your class about something you listened to in English. Then ask learners for recommendations. Notice how many join in by the second week.

dek: Unit 32 of 100: listening deserves the same scaled, autonomous input programme as reading — with its own distinct challenges around access, pace, and material choice.

aims.x: This unit does for listening what Unit 31 did for reading. It argues that listening needs its own large-scale, learner-chosen input programme, and it addresses the problems particular to the ear: speed, audio quality, access to devices and the pull towards subtitles.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why extensive listening has lagged behind extensive reading;
adapt Day and Bamford’s principles for listening;
choose graded audio, learner podcasts and authentic media in a sensible sequence;
train learners to use playback controls and subtitles strategically;
set up a light listening log and a regular schedule;
balance listening for pleasure with the staged listening lessons of Unit 3;
link extensive listening to connected speech (Unit 4).

why: Why this matters. Listening is often the most under-practised skill outside class. An extensive listening programme closes that gap the way extensive reading closes it for text.

background.x: Listening is often called the neglected skill. In many classrooms it is tested more than taught: learners hear a recording once or twice and answer questions, and the lesson moves on. John Field (2008) criticized this ‘comprehension approach’ and argued for teaching the processes of listening. Larry Vandergrift and Christine Goh (2012) showed how metacognitive training, in which learners plan, monitor and evaluate their listening, can make learners more effective listeners. Both lines of work concern intensive listening. Extensive listening, by contrast, is about quantity: hours of comprehensible spoken English.

Listening poses a problem that reading does not. A reader can slow down, reread and look back; a listener faces a stream of sound that does not wait. For most of the twentieth century, listening outside class also depended on radio schedules or expensive equipment. Willy Renandya and Thomas Farrell (2011), in an article whose title quotes a learner’s complaint that ‘the tape is too fast’, argue that learners’ difficulties often come from too little listening practice and that extensive listening at an easy level deserves a regular place in courses. Studies such as Chang and Millett (2014) report gains in listening fluency when learners listen repeatedly to graded audiobooks, although the research base is still smaller than for reading.

Access has changed. Many families in India now have at least one smartphone, even where a school has no computer lab, and free sources such as learner podcasts, radio archives and graded-reader audio are widely available. Access remains uneven, however, and data costs are real, so a programme must allow downloads, shared devices and offline audio. The NCF 2023 gives listening and speaking an important place in language learning from the earliest stages (NCERT 2023). Learners in multilingual India are already expert listeners across languages; they follow Hindi films, Tamil radio or Telugu news without effort. Extensive listening aims to build the same effortless familiarity with spoken English.

items: Listening log totals. Minutes per week over a term, as evidence of habit.
Weekly retell. A short pair retelling, observed with a simple checklist.
Listening fluency check. Learners listen to an easy story once at normal speed and summarize it; repeat each term.
Strategy survey. Learners report which playback and subtitle strategies they use.
How much English do your learners hear outside class each week?
What access do they have to devices, data and audio at home?
Do you test listening more than you teach it?
How do your learners use subtitles now?
Which Indian English sources could you add to the listening ladder?
What do you listen to in English for pleasure?

Model dialogues and logs are original. Song lyrics and broadcast transcripts must not be reproduced without permission. terms.def: News, interviews, podcasts and other audio or video made for general audiences rather than learners, usually introduced after graded audio and learner podcasts in a listening sequence.
An approach to teaching listening that places understanding before speaking, giving learners extensive listening before they are asked to produce language.
Natural, fluent speech in which sounds in neighbouring words change, link or disappear, as when want to becomes wanna; learners need practice in hearing it.

Listening to large amounts of easy, enjoyable material, such as graded audio, podcasts or radio, for general meaning and pleasure. It builds listening fluency and complements shorter, intensive listening lessons.
Listening material, such as audiobooks of graded readers, written and recorded within a controlled vocabulary and grammar level, so that learners can listen extensively with ease.
Close, focused listening to a short passage for specific detail or language features, usually with tasks and replays, as distinct from extensive listening.
A simple record kept by learners of their extensive listening, noting what they listened to, for how long, what they understood and what they would like to hear next.
An approach to teaching listening that develops learners’ awareness of the listening process and their control of strategies such as predicting, monitoring and evaluating (Vandergrift and Goh 2012).
The functions on an audio or video player, such as pause, replay and slowing down, that learners can use strategically to make listening manageable.

A viewing routine in which learners watch a clip without subtitles, then with English subtitles, then without again, so that the subtitled viewing supports understanding and the final viewing tests listening.
